title: Nullstellensatz for an algebra with fewer generators than the cardinality of the field
statement: Let $F$ be a field [def-weil-field], let $A$ be a commutative $F$-algebra, and let $(a_i)_{i\in I}$ be a family generating $A$ as an $F$-algebra, meaning that every element of $A$ is a polynomial expression in finitely many $a_i$ with coefficients in $F$ [def-weil-pbc-mv-polynomial-ring]. Suppose $|I|<|F|$. Then (1) for every maximal ideal $\mathfrak m$ of $A$, the quotient field $A/\mathfrak m$ is algebraic over $F$, meaning each of its elements satisfies a nonzero polynomial over $F$; and (2) $A$ is a Jacobson ring, meaning every prime ideal of $A$ is the intersection of the maximal ideals containing it. The zero algebra and finite fields are allowed; no finite-generation hypothesis on $I$ is imposed.

source.place: Tag 00FU (theorem-uncountable-nullstellensatz), clauses (1) and (2); at a maximal ideal the residue field is the quotient field A/m. Tag 046V (lemma-base-change-Jacobson) uses this theorem on the generators coming from the original algebra.

proof.text: First suppose $I$ is finite. The generation hypothesis makes $A$ a finite type $F$-algebra [def-weil-pbc-finite-type-algebra], so [lem-weil-pbc-finite-type-over-field-prime-intersection-maximal] proves (2), including when $A=0$. For any maximal $\mathfrak m$, [lem-weil-common-extension-fields-quotient-field] makes $K=A/\mathfrak m$ a field, generated by the images of the finitely many $a_i$. By [lem-weil-pbc-zariski-lemma], $K$ has a finite $F$-basis $W$, say of size $d$. For $x\in K$, if $1,x,\ldots,x^d$ were independent, [lem-sfb-independent-family-spanning-cardinality] would give $d+1\le d$. Thus there is a nontrivial relation among these powers, a nonzero polynomial annihilating $x$. This proves (1) in the finite case. This part requires no cardinal restriction on the finite family.

source.place: Tag 00FU, first sentence of the proof, using Tag 00FV (theorem-nullstellensatz); finite-dimensionality implies algebraicity by the displayed powers argument.

proof.text: Now assume $I$ is infinite. We first prove a claim for any field $K$ generated as an $F$-algebra by a family $(b_i)_{i\in I}$. For each finitely supported $e:I\to\mathbf N$, put $b^e=\prod_i b_i^{e(i)}$, with empty product $1$. The set $W=\{b^e:e\in\mathcal M(I)\}$ spans $K$: expand each polynomial expression for an element of $K$ into its finitely many monomials [def-weil-pbc-mv-polynomial-ring]. By [lem-sfb-monomial-index-cardinality], $|\mathcal M(I)|=|I|$, hence $|W|\le|I|$ (choose one exponent vector representing each element of $W$). If $x\in K$ were transcendental over $F$, [lem-sfb-transcendental-reciprocals-independent] would give an independent family indexed by all of $F$. Applying [lem-sfb-independent-family-spanning-cardinality] to this family and the spanning set $W$ gives $|F|\le|W|\le|I|<|F|$, a contradiction. Thus every element of $K$ is algebraic over $F$. The same claim holds with any infinite index set $J$ of size $|I|$ in place of $I$, by reindexing along a bijection.

source.place: Tag 00FU, monomial-counting and transcendental-multiplication paragraphs; Tag 00FT proof supplies the reciprocal family. We apply the independent/spanning comparison directly, avoiding a separate cardinal-dimension formalism.

proof.text: For every maximal ideal $\mathfrak m$ of $A$, its quotient $K=A/\mathfrak m$ is a field by [lem-weil-common-extension-fields-quotient-field], and is generated as an $F$-algebra by the images of the $a_i$: lift an element of the quotient to $A$ and reduce its polynomial expression. Step 2 therefore proves that $A/\mathfrak m$ is algebraic over $F$. Together with step 1, clause (1) is now proved universally under the hypotheses of the item; its proof uses no Jacobson assertion. If $A=0$, there are no maximal or prime ideals and both conclusions are vacuous.

source.place: Tag 00FU, first assertion; working directly in the quotient algebra instead of first reducing to a polynomial ring.

For clause (2) with $I$ infinite, fix a prime ideal $\mathfrak p$ of $A$ and $f

e0$, so $B
e0$: the defining fraction relation would make $1/1=0/1$ imply $g^k=0$ for some $k$, impossible in $D$. Choose a maximal ideal $\mathfrak n$ of $B$ by [lem-weil-common-extension-fields-maximal-ideal], and put $L=B/\mathfrak n$, a field by [lem-weil-common-extension-fields-quotient-field]. Every fraction in $B$ is $d g^{-r}$, and every $d$ is a polynomial in the images of the $a_i$. Hence these images together with $g^{-1}$ generate $B$, and their images generate $L$. The index set $I\sqcup\{*\}$ has cardinality $|I|$ because $I$ is infinite (shift a countably infinite subset by one place). Thus step 2, applied to this field $L$, shows $L/F$ algebraic.

source.place: Tag 00FU, last paragraph, localization by one additional generator. We choose a maximal residue field of (A/p)_f directly instead of using the non-Jacobson witness of Tag 034J.

source.place: Tag 00GA (lemma-finite-residue-extension-closed), proof, its intermediate-ring field argument written out; used at the end of Tag 00FU.

proof.text: For every prime $\mathfrak p$, all maximal ideals containing it contain each element of $\mathfrak p$. Conversely, for each $f\notin\mathfrak p$, steps 4-5 give one such maximal ideal omitting $f$. Hence their intersection is exactly $\mathfrak p$. This is the stated Jacobson property and completes (2) for $I$ infinite.

source.place: Tag 00FU, conclusion; the prime-intersection formulation follows from the maximal ideal avoiding f constructed in steps 4-5.
